extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, patent agents, law students, and judges
extracted.subtask_description: Legal standards governing false marking/false stamping of articles and the statutory and equitable methods for correcting defects in patents (clerical errors, disclaimers, re-issue), including remedies, procedures, and limits on amendment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intent to deceive required for false marking
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute's penalty is incurred by marking an unpatented article with the word 'patent' ... it must also appear that the article was so falsely marked with intent to deceive the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intent or purpose to deceive is ordinarily a question for the jury; the falsehood is a badge of fraud and a presumption of intent arises 'until the contrary appears.' Examples: marking in jest or ridicule (where no one could be misled) is not an offense; marking a dog or horse with 'patent' hardly shows intent to deceive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marking that cannot deceive or is obviously not patentable is not an offense
rubrics_metrics.description: That to mark 'patented' on articles evidently not patentable and which cannot deceive the public is not an offence (see U. S. v. Morris (1866)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasts with cases where marking was intended to deceive; Nichols v. Newell allows marking 'patented' where patent expected if no intent to deceive. Marking that cannot plausibly mislead the public is not punished.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offence committed by the act of false marking itself
rubrics_metrics.description: The offence is committed by marking falsely, not by carrying such marked articles into another district with intent to sell.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law (Pentlarge v. Kirby (1884)) holds the physical act of stamping/marking falsely creates the offence; sales or transport are not required elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Penalty and qui tam procedure for false stamping
rubrics_metrics.description: The punishment for violation is a fine of one hundred dollars and costs, to be recovered by any person in a qui tam action brought to the District Court of the United States within whose jurisdiction the offence may have been committed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural rules: the suit must be brought in the name of the informer (not the United States); the suit must be maintained in the district where the stamping was done (not merely where goods were sold); the full penalty may be imposed for each article falsely stamped and sold; in New York a pleading 'on or about the month of' is sufficient; in civil suits plaintiff is not bound to prove his case as fully as under indictment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venue and proof rules for false stamping suits
rubrics_metrics.description: A suit for false stamping under the relevant statute can be maintained only in the district where the stamping was done, and the plaintiff is not required to prove the case as fully as in a criminal indictment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited cases: Pentlarge v. Kirby, Winne v. Snow, Tompkins v. Butterfield. The plaintiff need not allege the tort happened on a specific day; 'on or about' is sufficient. The charge of false stamping must be proved beyond reasonable doubt in some contexts (see Tompkins v. Butterfield).

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate liability and agency for false stamping
rubrics_metrics.description: A corporation is liable for the act of its superintendent in wrongfully stamping if he knew or should have known that the article was not patented; acts of employees in false stamping are acts of the principal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Tompkins v. Butterfield; Kass v. Hawlowetz; where the stamping is done by an agent with general control service on a foreign corporation is sufficient upon the managing agent (Hat-Sweat Mfg. Co. v. Davis Sewing Mach. Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible marking where patent expired or patent date included
rubrics_metrics.description: Articles may be marked 'patented' and may so be marked although the patent has expired, if the date of the patent is included in the mark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases such as Wilson v. Singer Mfg. Co. allow marking with patent date even after expiration; but marking after expiration with intent to deceive (or marking without appropriate date to mislead) may be actionable under Sec. 4900.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical duty of alien inventor to put invention into U.S. market
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the act of 1886 an alien inventor and patentee had a duty to put his patented invention into the market in the United States within eighteen months after issue of the patent; 'to put into market' consisted in offering it for sale at a reasonable price.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to do so forfeited his right to recover for infringement; this requirement did not extend to native assignees of an alien patentee and was later removed (act of 1870 and subsequent changes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee bound by patent language as construed by courts
rubrics_metrics.description: The protection afforded by a patent is limited and defined by the language it employs for describing and claiming the invention, as that language is interpreted by the courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the patent language fails to cover the actual invention (too much or too little), the patentee may be defeated in securing rights; claiming more than invention may be treated as fraud on the public; claiming too little or incorrect description may be fraudulent concealment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendment power cannot change invention's nature or patentee's identity
rubrics_metrics.description: The power to amend defective language of a patent does not include the power to change the nature of the patented invention or the person of the patentee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An amended patent cannot be transformed into a grant for a different invention or to a different person; any change that affects the essential character of the invention or the person entitled requires a new original patent application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three classes of patent defects and their remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Defects are divided into (1) clerical errors; (2) errors consisting in an excess of claim; and (3) errors of any kind in matters relating to the substance of the grant; remedies: (1) corrected by action of the Patent Office; (2) cured by disclaimer; (3) removed by re-issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The second class (excess of claim) overlaps the third insofar as substance is concerned but has a peculiar remedy (disclaimer) in addition to re-issue. Each remedy and method of application is treated separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clerical errors: definition and correction procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Clerical errors include mistakes in the patent that do not affect the substance of the grant and occur through the fault of Patent Office employees; upon discovery the patentee may apply to the Commissioner and, if clearly shown by Office records, a certificate correcting the error will be signed by the Secretary and countersigned by the Commissioner and endorsed on the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A printed copy of the certificate is attached to printed specifications and drawings; correction of clerical error relates back to the date of the patent but cannot affect intervening rights; examples include errors in numbers or Christian names if identity remains clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive errors cannot be corrected as clerical errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Errors affecting the substance of the grant cannot be corrected in the summary manner reserved for clerical errors and must be removed by re-issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When re-issue is required through official negligence, no fees are charged for allowance unless the re-issue operates as an amendment of defects beyond those for which the Patent Office is responsible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclaimer: purposes, statutory distinction, and effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclaimer serves two purposes: (a) as a method of amending a defective patent (Sec. 4917) and (b) as a method by which a plaintiff in an infringement suit may avoid the defence that his original patent claimed more than his invention and still recover damages (Sec. 4922).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These provisions are distinct and have different scopes. A disclaimer is an abandonment of an apparent right, may be filed by any owner of the whole or a sectional interest, and as modified by the disclaimer the original patent is thereafter construed in cases where the disclaimant's rights are involved. A disclaimer does not admit the patent is void.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excessive claim: definition and methods of ascertainment
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is excessive when it claims any material and substantial thing beyond the scope of the real invention of the patentee or beyond what he has described in specification, drawings, or model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immaterial or unessential features are not regarded as covered. To ascertain excess compare claims to descriptions on the face of the patent and investigate identity of invention by foreign patents, actual use (discarded features), or other evidence showing features were known at date of invention. If excess is separable it may be disclaimed; if not separable the whole claim is void and re-issue is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excessive claim amendable by disclaimer only if mistake without fraud
rubrics_metrics.description: An excessive claim can be amended by disclaimer only when the error arose through inadvertence, accident, or mistake, and without any fraudulent or deceptive intention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The law requires utmost good faith and reasonable diligence in drafting claims; a patentee who willfully inserts or persists in unlawful claims is not aided by disclaimer and risks rejection of the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excessive claim amendable by disclaimer only if amended claim is patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: An excessive claim can be amended by disclaimer only when the claim as amended would cover a patentable invention; the patentee has no right to any patent unless he has invented something lawfully patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the portion rightfully claimed is not a material and substantial part of the invention, disclaimer is ineffectual; disclaimer cannot rescue a patent where the remaining claim would not be patentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core rules limiting amending power (inexorable rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three rules cannot be affected by the amending power: (1) the invention must have existed at the issue of the original patent (clearly perceived as well as conceived and fully reduced to practice); (2) the original application must have attempted to describe and claim every attribute the inventor desired to bring within the monopoly; (3) the monopoly created by the patent must be commensurate with the invention the inventor then endeavored to protect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These rules preclude introducing into an amended patent any patentable matter not clearly in the inventor's mind or not reduced to practice at the original issue; they distinguish amended patents from new original patents and preserve public rights.
